Definitions and the representative relaxationThe distinction between an actual partial sub-quorum colouring and a feasible representative pair is handled correctly.Let  $C$  be the coloured support. The sub-quorum condition is
$$\bigl|\{u\in N[v]\cap C:\operatorname{col}(u)=\operatorname{col}(v)\}\bigr|
\ \ge\ \frac{|N[v]\cap C|}{2}
\qquad(v\in C).$$
Thus the vertex itself counts, uncoloured vertices do not count, and equality at one half is allowed. All three points matter to the construction.Why  $\beta_2\le\psi_{\rm sq}$ Give every vertex of a dissociation set a different colour. Each coloured vertex has at most one other coloured neighbour, so its coloured closed neighbourhood has size at most two. Its own colour occupies one vertex, which meets the required half.Why  $\psi_{\rm sq}\le\Omega$ From any partial sub-quorum colouring, retain:One edge from every colour class containing an edge.One vertex from every edge-free colour class.Edges retained from different colour classes are vertex-disjoint, so they form a matching  $M$ . Its endpoints  $P$  are disjoint from the retained singleton set  $T$ .For  $t\in T$ , the original colour class was edge-free. Consequently, the only vertex of its own colour in its original coloured closed neighbourhood was  $t$  itself. Sub-quorum therefore gives
$$1\ge \frac{|N[t]\cap C|}{2},$$
and hence
$$|N(t)\cap C|\le1.$$
Retaining a subset of  $C$  cannot increase that number, so
$$|N(t)\cap(T\cup P)|\le1.$$
This is exactly the stated representative feasibility condition.The pair has one unit of  $|T|+|M|$  per original colour. Therefore  $\psi_{\rm sq}\le\Omega$ .Crucially, this argument imposes no sub-quorum condition on the retained matching endpoints. Arbitrary feasible representative pairs need not produce valid colourings. The upper bound is proved for that larger feasible class, and the lower-bound construction is separately checked as an actual colouring. There is no conflation of the two notions.3. =|T|+\frac{|P|}{2}

6. Structural hypothesesMedianityThe initial ladder is  $P_n\square K_2$ , a median graph: its median is obtained coordinatewise from the path medians.The square-attachment argument also holds. For a median graph  $B$  and an edge  $de$ , consider
$$X=(V(B)\times\{0\})\cup(\{d,e\}\times\{1\})$$
inside  $B\square K_2$ . The two layer-one vertices are the added vertices.The induced subgraph on  $X$  is isometric:Between layer-zero vertices, a shortest path in  $B$  remains available.From  $(d,1)$  to  $(x,0)$ , crossing to  $(d,0)$  and following a shortest path in  $B$  achieves the product distance  $1+d_B(d,x)$ .The same applies starting at  $(e,1)$ .The two layer-one vertices are adjacent.It is also closed under the ambient coordinatewise median. If the median’s second coordinate is zero, it belongs to  $X$ . If that coordinate is one, at least two input vertices are in layer one. Their first coordinates lie in  $\{d,e\}$ , and the first-coordinate median lies in their interval, which is contained in  $\{d,e\}$ .Thus the ambient median lies in  $X$ . Isometry preserves the relevant intervals, and uniqueness follows from uniqueness in the ambient median graph. Each attachment therefore preserves medianity, proving it for every  $H_r$ .Outerplanarity and two-connectivityThe stated drawing works: top ears lie outside the top row, bottom ears outside the bottom row, and their horizontal intervals are disjoint.More explicitly, the outer boundary is a spanning cycle:Traverse the top row from left to right, replacing each ear’s root edge by its new length-three path.Cross the last rung.Traverse the bottom row from right to left, making the same replacements.Cross the first rung.This cycle contains every vertex. The retained root edges and internal rungs have a noncrossing embedding inside it. Hence the graph is outerplanar.The spanning cycle also proves two-connectivity directly: deleting any vertex leaves a spanning path through all remaining vertices. The manuscript’s attachment-based deletion argument is valid as well.Order, degrees and the extra automorphism claimThere are  $2n$  old vertices and  $n$  ears adding two vertices each, for  $4n=16r$  vertices.Every old vertex gains exactly one neighbour:The four old corners have degree three.All other old vertices have degree four.All new vertices have degree two.Since  $n\ge4$ , noncorner old vertices exist, so the maximum degree is exactly four.The additional automorphism assertion is also correct. In a corner ear, the two new degree-two vertices would have to map to one another under any automorphism sending every vertex to a neighbour. Their old neighbours would then have to be interchanged, contradicting their respective degrees three and four.These are not full rectangular grids. A rectangular grid with both dimensions at least three has exactly four degree-two vertices, whereas  $H_r$  has  $2n=8r$  degree-two vertices. A two-row rectangular grid has maximum degree at most three. The theorem therefore does not settle the rectangular-grid conjecture.7. Independence of the literal reference computationsThe two exact routines are independent of the local-budget proof in the relevant algorithmic sense.literal(g)This routine receives only adjacency data. It tests dissociation and formation directly from their definitions. It does not use the ear partition, the two-per-square conclusion, exceptional squares or an assumed optimum.Its minimality test is correct. For every selected vertex  $v$ , the deletion mask
$$s\mathbin{\hat{~}}(1\ll v)=s-2^v$$
is numerically smaller than  $s$ , so its forming status has already been recorded.Testing single deletions is sufficient because formation is upward closed: enlarging the selected set preserves previously selected neighbours and cannot deactivate a selected vertex. If any proper subset of  $S$  were forming, some single-deletion subset of  $S$  containing it would also be forming.The local variable named sf stores the maximum minimal-forming-set size, correctly reported as "SF". Its name is potentially confusing, but its calculation is correct.exact_omega(g)The edge list contains each undirected edge once. The recursion chooses edges in increasing index order and rejects shared endpoints. Every matching therefore has exactly one recursion path, including the empty matching.For a fixed endpoint set  $P$ , it allows  $T$  only from
$$A(P)=\{v\notin P:|N(v)\cap P|\le1\}.$$
This filter follows directly from feasibility: a vertex with two  $P$ -neighbours cannot satisfy the required bound after any further vertices are added to  $T$ .Every subset of  $A(P)$  is generated, and the routine then tests the full condition
$$|N(t)\cap(P\cup T)|\le1\qquad(t\in T).$$
It maximizes  $|M|+|T|$  without using the square classification, interval bound or expected answer nine to prune the search.The 1,369,324 masks therefore are tested candidate masks after a necessary filter, including candidates subsequently rejected as infeasible. They are not a count of feasible pairs alone.Both exact routines share the same graph constructor. Their independence is from the proof’s counting logic; it is not a claim of independently implemented graph models. Inspection confirms that the shared constructor matches the mathematical definition.8. Material clarifications onlyNo mathematical repair or checker modification is required. I recommend only these clarifications:Use “maximum degree four” in abbreviated theorem statements. The manuscript already states this correctly.Replace “next block” by “adjacent block, when present.” At a left boundary the relevant block is the previous one.
